projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Jose Lionel Cortez was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Daniel Ruiz
sp.p: The veteran's name is Jose Lionel Cortez. His birthday is 11/9/1926. He served in the U.S. Army. The highest rank achieved was a T5 Corporal. It is November 2, 2008, we are in Donna, Texas. This is my Grandpa. My name is Daniel Ruiz and this is being conducted for hte veteran's history project at the Library of Congress.

sp.speaker: Jose Lionel Cortez
sp.p: In 1945 and I, well went in early to the army because I had a buddy and myself who were running around together, working together and everything, and he told me one day he was 18 and had to go register for the draft. So I was 17 so I said I'll go with you.

sp.speaker: Daniel Ruiz
sp.p: So you weren't old enough?

sp.speaker: Jose Lionel Cortez
sp.p: Well we walked in to the recruiting office there in Weslaco and they saw that we were there. The recruiting officer he said that you guys 18? Yes Sir. So we both I went in when I was 17. And we both thought that we would be able to stay together in the army but no. We got to the San Antonio recruiting office there. Alex went one way and I went the other way.

sp.speaker: Daniel Ruiz
sp.p: What was his name?

sp.speaker: Jose Lionel Cortez
sp.p: Hm?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ruiz
sp.p: What was his name? Your friend?

sp.speaker: Jose Lionel Cortez
sp.p: Yeah

sp.speaker: Daniel Ruiz
sp.p: Alex?

sp.speaker: Jose Lionel Cortez
sp.p: Yeah, and I didn't see Alex till he got back and I got back. And I went to a they sent a group of us to a little camp here in Texas. It use to be Camp Walters and for training. So we were there in training camp for a while and later on we had one morning, you know, we had everybody checks in and they had role call and everything. The officer said that they were going to call off some names, and then we're going to we would have to stand off to one side so they kept calling names and my name came out so I had to walk over there and stand with the other people you know. And from there I don't know why they separate because we weren't through with training. So they took us over there to Fort Jackson in Florida we stayed there for about 3 weeks or so from there they I don't know why why they separated us, probably might have sented us to a special assignment or something, but anyway. After that was out of fort what was the name? In Florida Jacksonville in Florida. We some of us went I went to Fort Bragg North Carolina. And I was a farm boy you know. I didn't know much about anything. I didn't have much of an education because I didn't get to finish school. We had to work, so they put me to work there in Fort Bragg in a section that checks the people that go AWOL, that disappear from the army. You know, like I said, I didn't know too much, but I had a good, I always had a good computer so they they I had a good Lieutenant. I still remember his name, Lieutenant Simbison. He was a Jewish person, but he was good. Anyway I had about I learn quickly because I have always been able to do that and I was second in command in the office, you know we had about I don't know ten or twelve female workers there so the Lieutenant put me in command so he was second in command and I stayed there for the duration of the war, I didn't I didn't get to go over seas, and there was a bunch of us you know, and every pay day we got together and went to Fairfield North Carolina which was the town closes to Fort Bragg, and had a good time and had a ball there all the time. Anyway, I learned a lot, I asked the Lieutenant if I could stay after hours you know so I learned how to type I use to type 60-70 words a minute, I learned by myself. And I advanced, and I got accustomed to working in the office, and directing people and everything and that helped me a lot in the future of my life you know. And during the we didn't do anything. I had a permanent pass we went into the service there in Fort Bragg and but you were working in the office, you didn't have any revity, you didn't have to wake up in the morning and role call or anything like that. We had a we could after five 0' clock we could take off and gO and don't corne back till eight o'clock in the morning so I had a good time and I learned a lot, I learned in the army my service in the military changed I think my life my direction of where I was going you know what I was going to do. Anyway during world war when the war ended the we all everybody went out to celebrate and after that you know right after the war they start bringing lots of people from over seas. And they put a Lieutenant who had been through the war and he'd been wounded you know he was disabled not completely disabled but he wa" disabled and then he was second in command to the Lieutenant. So pretty soon you know they start mustering out all the people you know mustering out mustering out because they are going to be discharged. So I was discharged and carne back horne back horne, when I was in there, Fort Bragg, the civil senrice they called it at that time, asked me if i wanted to stay and work in the arn1Y for the civil senrice, a government job you know. I said no, I want to go horne. So I carne horne, like I said I think that the procedures that I went in through in the army showed me discipline and how to how to get ahead how to think how to do things vou know. So I carne back. I don't remember exactly but anywav I came back from the war I got a discharge and everything. A honorable discharge I still have a little bit of it

sp.speaker: Daniel Ruiz
sp.p: How long were yOU in the army?

sp.speaker: Jose Lionel Cortez
sp.p: Hm?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ruiz
sp.p: How long?

sp.speaker: Jose Lionel Cortez
sp.p: In the army? Not quite two years.

sp.speaker: Daniel Ruiz
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Jose Lionel Cortez
sp.p: Yeah, after the war ended all the people were let go you know, most of the people some people wanted to stay, but I didn't want to stay, I wanted to go horne. Like I said, my my direction I think wa." completely changed by my service in the military because I learned like I told you discipline and how to do things and how to think you know how to think solve problems and other things. So I came home and my duration in the army wasn't wasn't that long. There was no, no serious we volunteered tOOos voliemos a bunch of guys that we use to run around together every time they had a something in the bulletin board you know us group of volunteers we went and volunteered. But one time they they took a bunch of us and took us back to Florida and we stayed there about 3 or 4 weeks. We were suppose to go on a special assignment. But no they sent us back to Fort Bragg. But I don't remember why but I had my service in the military was very short. My friend Alex he went to the front in Germany. Alex told me you know when he when he came back and I came back when he was going to walking to the front lines you know where the combat was going on there's Germans, dead Germans all over the place. And the battle was raging on you know and I probably would have been somewhere in there ifT hadn't been pulled from my training camp I don't know why, it just wasn't my time. And like I said my military service was really shon. Okay. That's about it, I didn't complete my basic training like I told you, they took us out of there a bunch of us. I didn't remember how many either 15 or 20. Took us out oftraining like I said they sent us to Fort jackson in Florida and from there to Forr Bragg and thars where I spent the entire war. fr was a shorr rime thar I was in the militarv you know. not quite 2 years that I was in the milirary.

sp.speaker: Daniel Ruiz
sp.p: Would you want to do it again? Would you like to re-enlist?

sp.speaker: Jose Lionel Cortez
sp.p: No. no I didn't have any intention of re-enlisting or anything bur I should have stayed in the military because when you know by the time I was 40. Less than 40. 37 years old I would have had a permanent retirement. Yeah but I didn't. But one thing I did have in the military I have obtained a lot of benefits. Being a veteran serving during in a time of war even though you don't fight or go to the front, you still in the Army ar the time of war. They do an alias. So I didn't go to a VA to take care of my body you know until 1989. I was going blind and I went to a friend of mine who passed away already he told me as soon as I went to work at the garage and I was wiping the sweat from my eyes from my face and I closed this eye and opened this eye and I couldn't see nothing. I mean completely blind so Edward Cardenas like I said he is already passed away and he told me, you're a veteran Lionel, go to the VA over there on North 10th and McCullough. And so I did. I had to go. I went the next day and I told I don't the guy I see him every once in a while. He told me. you tell them in there that you need a hospital. So then they would take yoU but I was non combat so I did. I told the doctor when I went in there the doctor Ie digo I'm corning to see you if you never come to the VA before but I needed to go to a hospital because I'm going blind so he looked imo my eyes and yeah he called right away. He called San Antonio. And they sent me away over there to get some laser treatment on my eyes. They saved my vision. But they ruined my left eye.

sp.speaker: Daniel Ruiz
sp.p: Oh really?

sp.speaker: Jose Lionel Cortez
sp.p: Yeah. I can see but they did that young lady that was working at the laser gun. Some how or I don't know what happened she made a hot shot right in the center of my eye and that it scarred so that keeps me from seeing perfect. But my eye here is they saved my vision and because at least I can see with this, but it's getting weaker so pretty soon I won't be able to work or anything like that to read or write anyway from watching TV some of the letters I see on TV are kind of blurred.

sp.speaker: Daniel Ruiz
sp.p: How old are you? How old are you?

sp.speaker: Jose Lionel Cortez
sp.p: Now?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ruiz
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jose Lionel Cortez
sp.p: I'll be 82 on the 6th of November, still strong, I'm still strong. I take care of my body, that's an essential thing you need to do, a primary thing you got to do, take care of your body cuz there's not enough gold in the world to buy a body. You can repair it but you cannot get another one so you got take care of your body. Life is beautiful got you got to stay healthy got to stay healthy. Thats about it, it was something that helped me, when I came back I was still a uniformer on every Sunday. I was I use to live with my aunts you know in a right in the ranch general home is right behind the the that building, I use to stay with my aunts, I was walking down there and I saw a door open at the back of the store, a man unpacking furniture so I came around walked back. And I asked the man that I was just got out of the Army I said I was looking for a job, come Monday.

sp.speaker: Daniel Ruiz
sp.p: Wow!

sp.speaker: Jose Lionel Cortez
sp.p: That's all he said so I worked there for pretty close to 15-16 years in that furniture store. So I And I learned how to do more things and eventually by the time I got out of the the people died, owner died, died I was a manager at the store I was taking care of everything and it happened that the este used to buy furniture and go to Chicago for a month or two, we use to own the store, me and Henry Semota. So when Henry passcd away they sold, Thelma sold the store you know, that was Henry's wife. The other guy didnt ______. I got out of there.

sp.speaker: Daniel Ruiz
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Jose Lionel Cortez
sp.p: Yeah. But that's a long story, this is a day. I have a paper read you know I read it. when I got _______. _______friend of mine said that if I wanted to go, no that was after that. I was staying at uptown, here in the garage station, and a police car came by. And the guy said the officer driving _______. _______ job. one day. And he took me to the police station and told me you were going to be the new radio dispatcher. Yeah, and I quickly learned how to do it and everything and I worked there for quite some time, quite sometime. And then from dispatcher, I got promoted to police officer. One day the chief was having trouble with the Chief of Administration and they they fired the chief and they told me, the police department that "we are going to quit the fire chief", but you can stay here. So I stayed as a dispatcher, and thats when made me as a police officer you know so I worked there for a while. But that's another story the police work, I'll give you another statement later about the police work. Later you know on in the police work, the chief and I got over some personal problems, and he fired me. And I didn't want to, I did file a grievance with the city administration. I made an appointment. I was going to go in front of the city council with a plea you know, fight my case, which I did, but I don't know who but somebody called KRGV TV channelS, but I knew like I said they weren't going to do anything, but I walked the down the rows during a council meeting mayor and all the other commissioners, and I told them: well the way I see it you people are not going to hear me. I have no chance with you. I was walking around the table, and I will tell you one thing, you people are not worth the dollar the city pays you a year, and I walked out of there. Later a guy that I knew was the police chief well I want you to come work with me as assistant chief of police. Okay! It's, it's my knee hurts. It don't matter, you still come to work. I came in the next day and I was there for a long time in police work. And I got to be assistant chief because I was tired of assistant chief, and I was already chief police and I stayed there tor quite awhile.

sp.speaker: Daniel Ruiz
sp.p: And you didn't have any high school or anything?

sp.speaker: Jose Lionel Cortez
sp.p: Hm?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ruiz
sp.p: Did you have any school education?

sp.speaker: Jose Lionel Cortez
sp.p: No. I went to, went to police school training here in Donna, yeah I had gone to the academy, in Alamo Academy, but you learn a lot by yourself just by plain old common sense. So I stayed there in Alamo for quite a while. They even made me the chief of police. A lot of experiences, a lot of danger, I went through a lot. One day I had hired a young man, a young man about your age maybe. So I hired Otenio Garza. And put him through school and everything, got him trained. But he was quickly to learn. But I made him assistant chief. About that time, something happened you know, the city administration had hired a city manager, or administrator, and so right away I knew something was wrong with this guy. I kept on thinking something was wrong with this guy so I kept my eye on him and I went to Otenio one morning, the guy had gone up somewhere with one of the city crews I had looked at his license plate in the start, it looked all crumbled up and everything, an old California plate. So I told Otenio, and I said to chief Otenio you get those numbers of the license plate plates and run it 10-28, 10-29, that's, that's the procedure was used to identify the vehicle where it's from and the record of the driver and everything like that, the owner. Otenio came back all excited, chief! Chief! Chief! This guy's a fugitive! We had a big criminal, he had a long record in California, and arrest warrants all over the place. So at that time the guy was walking in, so I told Otenio. Mr. Garza, you put this man under arrest, read him his rights, put him in jail book him and put him in jail and transfer him to the county jail, but it's in there. I went over and told the mayor hey, I have your city manager in jail. What do you mean? He had a long criminal record from California. We checked on him and he's one of those with a bunch of arrest warrants on him. This guy here was smart, he could talk. He was working for a government agency in McAllen. The Lower Rio Grande Development Company, and he had hired him without checking background. And this guy was a big big criminal I mean we got him. But I had a lot of rewards, a lot of danger a lot of stuff. But I quit the police chief job when I bought the garage in 1979. And I've been there ever since, and hopefully another couple of years. I don't know how long my eyes are going to last so I'll have to have burn up some of my relatives support me. No everything's alright but I went through a lot of police work, a lot of experiences. It went to a lot of things. People die. It could go one way we get shot, another. We were living in a little house over there with Maria's relatives in Donna and a guy came and shot out the windows of my car. Because he was a big time criminal, burglar and everything about your age. Well that's about it hijo I have a lot of details from my police work.
